According to Mark Gurman's latest *Power On* newsletter, Apple is reportedly weighing a series of changes to the App Store. The goal? To boost its potential revenue.

It remains unclear exactly what changes Apple has in mind for the App Store. Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman reports that Apple wants to "find ways to improve profit margins and extract more recurring revenue from the platform," a push being driven largely by incoming CEO John Ternus and current services SVP Eddy Cue.

The move is said to be one of the reasons Phil Schiller, a long-serving Apple executive, departed last week. Schiller, who stepped down as SVP of marketing in 2020 to become an Apple Fellow, had oversight of the App Store among his duties. He was not in favor of the idea:

There are plenty of ways Apple could boost App Store margins. It could do away with the manual app review process, which in the age of agentic coding may be costly and not all that effective. Users would probably not appreciate further automated review, though, even if it would cut costs.

Top-rated SF comment

Considering Apple's fluctuating position as the world's most valuable company, if this rumor is true, it's terrible news and completely unnecessary. This could be a very dangerous signal for the new CEO. I was hoping that having someone with a hardware background in charge would bring us back to an Apple that puts products over services, but if this is true, it's a pointless and greedy move. I hope it's not true.

Apple could raise developer membership fees, currently $99 per year. Given that many small developers are already paying $200/month for subscriptions to Codex and Claude to build their apps, it's fair to say Apple could raise prices without anyone leaving. Apple could also charge high-traffic developers subscription fees, passing on some of the infrastructure costs.

Only time will tell how it all plays out, but I'm excited to see what changes might eventually come.

7c0870763cce.content:
一名流行文化播客主持人，就喺博彩平台 Polymarket 上推廣林賽·克蘭西（Lindsay Clancy）案投注一事公開道歉。

據《Variety》報道，主持「Not Skinny But Not Fat」節目嘅主持人 Amanda Hirsch，喺帖文入面標註 Polymarket 合作夥伴標籤，寫道：「喺 Polymarket 上面預測判決結果係無罪。你感到意外嗎？#Polymarketpartner」，隨即引發猛烈反彈。該篇喺星期五發佈嘅帖文已被刪除。

Hirsch 隨即遭到粉絲同聽眾嘅強烈批評，而佢而家就話嗰篇帖文「唔符合佢一貫嘅作風」。

Hirsch 星期日喺 Instagram 寫道：「將林賽·克蘭西案同品牌合作內容一齊講，實在係好唔體貼、好錯，而且完全唔似我平時嘅作風——我應該更加謹慎，而當時冇即時意識到呢一點令我感到非常難受。」該帖文嘅留言功能已經關閉。

佢繼續寫道，話自己「太過沉溺於」審訊報道之中，「完全失去咗應有嘅判斷力」，冇考慮到嗰篇帖文有幾「極度不當」。

Hirsch 寫道：「我做咗一個好差嘅決定，對此我感到非常難受。我知道刪除帖文都唔可以當冇事發生過。講真，我對自己嘅選擇感到好震驚，請大家明白呢次判斷失誤並唔代表我呢個人。我真係深感抱歉。」

克蘭西因為殺害自己三名年幼子女而受審。雖然辯方從未否認佢殺害子女嘅行為，但佢哋辯稱克蘭西喺犯案時正經歷產後精神病。然而控方就指，克蘭西喺殺害子女時能夠分辨是非，應該為相關死亡承擔刑事責任。

呢宗審訊喺社交媒體上引起廣泛關注，網民對判決結果應該係點睇法嚴重分歧。克蘭西嘅支持者喺法院外排隊表達支持，亦有人喺網上分享自己產後精神病同產後抑鬱嘅經歷，以示同情。

星期五，經過七日嘅商議，陪審團表示未能達成一致裁決，法官隨即宣布審判無效，需要重審。

呢宗案件仲引起咗總統特朗普嘅注意，佢同記者講呢件案係一件「羞恥」同「悲劇」。

特朗普星期五對記者講：「呢個情況真係好糟糕。睇吓，佢做咗一件好恐怖、好恐怖嘅事。冇可能更差，但你哋會知道要付出嘅代價係咩。總會有代價。最終可能會係入精神病院或者坐牢，或者其他安排，但我估佢哋會再進行一次審訊。實在太可惜。」

華盛頓（美聯社）——在一名聯邦法官阻止針對郵寄選票的新限制後,特朗普政府週日再次向最高法院提出上訴,事關中期選舉。

是次呈交文件,源於美國地方法院法官英迪拉・塔爾瓦尼延長一項命令,禁止郵政部門執行特朗普總統關於十一月大選的行政命令。

各州已陸續寄出郵寄選票之際,法律爭議隨之而來,令政府幾乎無時間對郵寄選票規則作出重大修改。

司法部長辦公室首席律師約翰・紹爾在文件中指出:「北卡羅來納州已開始寄出選票,隨着禁制令仍然生效,更多州將展開寄發程序,包括阿拉巴馬州將於九月九日開始,以及至少五個州在九月十三日當週跟進。」

「一旦選票信封進入郵遞系統,便無法追回。雖然禁制令容許郵政部門及各州繼續採取措施,確保信封符合有關規定的要求……但禁制令每維持一日,便可能引發混亂與亂局,因為禁制令令這些準備步驟變成自願性質,而非強制執行。」

是次上訴是政府第三次要求最高法院介入。最高法院一直容許有關計劃推進,但尚未就其合法性作出裁決。

這場角力可能對今年的選舉產生重大影響,國會控制權正是今次選舉的關鍵所在。美國近三分之一的選民以郵寄方式投票。

民主黨主政的州份及投票權利組織指稱,有關變動違反憲法。選舉官員則認為,現時並無足夠時間修改其制度以配合郵政部門的新指令。

特朗普政府一直將這些限制定位為符合常理、在其權力範圍內可對郵政作出的規管。

紹爾表示:「簡而言之,應對答辯人對未能遵守規則之憂慮的最佳方法,是即時批予行政層面的暫緩執行,繼而在進一步審議前全面暫緩執行。這將消除地方法院對規則所施加的不當不確定性,清楚向各方表明遵守規則並非可有可無,必須立即開始執行。」

特朗普長期試圖限制郵寄投票,儘管他本人亦經常以此方式投票。他曾就2020年大選敗予民主黨人喬・拜登一事,將責任錯誤歸咎於郵寄投票,散播毫無根據的舞弊指控。然而至今,他仍未能改變這項長久沿用的投票程序。

0fbaebe1f43b.content:
In the past few days, two reports have suggested that Apple could boost its profits by increasing services revenue in different ways.

In my view, Apple absolutely should pursue the first approach, but should not adopt the second — and it seems Phil Schiller may well agree with this stance...

Let me first summarise the content of these two reports.

Home Security and Monitoring Service

On Friday, *Bloomberg* reported that Apple may be planning to launch a brand-new home security and monitoring service, debuting alongside some of the new home hardware we have been expecting.

Extracting More Revenue from the App Store

Another report from the same source on Sunday indicated that the company is exploring ways to extract more revenue and profit from the App Store.

Apple Should Not Take the Latter Approach

Conversely, I believe the second approach would be a massive mistake.

Apple's effective monopoly over iPhone app sales has come under fierce attack from regulators around the world. In most countries, if you want to sell an app on an iPhone, you have to go through the official App Store, leaving you with no choice but to accept the company's terms.

I understand the common argument that no one is forcing anyone to buy an iPhone or develop apps for it, but that is not how even the most laissez-faire free-market economies actually work — the US has had antitrust laws since 1890. Once you reach a certain level of market dominance, regulators impose restrictions on your conduct to ensure you do not abuse your position.

Trying to squeeze more money out of the App Store runs exactly counter to "skating to where the puck is going." According to *Bloomberg*, Phil Schiller shares this view, and notes that it is one of the reasons for his current stepping back.

Innovative Services Are the Right Direction

By contrast, launching innovative services that people are happy to pay for is absolutely what Apple should be doing. I can easily see the value in the company offering a home security monitoring service.

I argued back in 2024 that developing its own smart home cameras would be one of the... wisest moves the company could make. I expressed the same view regarding rumours of an Apple smart doorbell. Offering an optional service bundle to go with security products makes sense on both fronts.

First, there are the privacy reasons I have mentioned many times before. HomeKit Secure Video has already made a major contribution to ensuring the privacy of security camera footage. If I had to pick one company I would trust to analyse security camera footage with AI, it would be Apple.

Second, Apple is of course best positioned to fully integrate security hardware and services within the HomeKit ecosystem. I am confident Apple can deliver similar benefits in many other areas as well.

For me, the key point is that Apple needs to treat services with the same approach it applies to hardware — build outstanding products that consumers are happy and willing to pay for, rather than extracting money in ways that leave customers, developers, and regulators alike unhappy.

What are your thoughts? Feel free to share your views in the comments.

The foldable design should make the iPhone Ultra Apple's most groundbreaking model yet. It will feature a wide book-style fold, with an outer display of roughly 5.4 inches and an inner display of 7.8 inches, similar to an iPad mini.

91de1b440b6c.content:
There have long been numerous rumours and reports suggesting that Apple is developing a foldable clamshell device, which could be an iPad, a Mac, or both — possibly even a hybrid of the two.

Recently there have been reports claiming that, although this was once a priority project for incoming CEO John Ternus, the plans have been cancelled — but I don't think that's entirely the truth...

Personally, I believe the concept of a Mac and iPad hybrid device has essentially been made obsolete by the times. Today's Macs can run iPhone and iPad apps, and for many people, iPhone Mirroring is another tool that achieves the same result. We are also seeing increasing convergence between the two operating systems, and I believe this trend will continue: Apple's old argument of "we don't believe in combining a toaster and a refrigerator" is long past its expiry date.

But I do believe that once the technology matures to the point where a soft keyboard can replace a hard one, we will eventually have an all-screen foldable Mac. This won't happen in the short term, but it will happen eventually.

The dynamic keyboard as an interim solution

The reason I believe this is still a long way off is that I think there will be an intermediate stage with dynamic hardware keyboards first. I discussed why I believe this is the direction of travel as long ago as a decade ago, and although such technology is in use in some niche applications today, it has still not entered the mainstream.

The Sonder Keyboard was one of the early attempts, using miniature e-ink displays to remap key labels and functions.

For example, for someone spending the day editing video in Final Cut Pro, a standard QWERTY keyboard is virtually useless, which is why physical keyboards and keyboard covers have always had a market.

How clever would it be if our MacBook keyboard or desktop Magic Keyboard could automatically adapt its labels to the application in use at the time?

Feels like a hard keyboard, but is a soft one

But the long-term goal is always a fully software-based keyboard. As I noted back in 2016, the arguments Steve Jobs made when introducing virtual keys with the iPhone apply equally to the Mac keyboard.

Of course, soft keyboards have three problems:

  • Glass keyboards don't feel comfortable to type on.
  • We rely on key travel for both feedback and comfort.
  • Touch typists need to be able to feel the position of keys before pressing them.

Apple already holds patents addressing each of these three problems. First, using a flexible display rather than conventional glass can create deformation when a virtual key is pressed. The second problem can be addressed by combining this deformation with haptic motors. Finally, for the issue of feeling physical keys with the fingers, there are two solutions.

Apple's patent uses electrostatic charges to make the user feel changes in surface texture. In other words, even if the surface remains flat, applying a charge to the display surface can make it feel as though physical keys are present. And in 2023, researchers at Carnegie Mellon University proposed an alternative approach.

It's a question of 'when', not 'if'

Of course, all of this technology is still at a very early stage, but we only need to look at the Mac trackpad to find a precedent. The trackpad still sounds and feels like a mechanical device, but in reality it has been a solid-state device simulating physical clicks through haptic technology for many years — and the effect is extremely convincing.

The soft keyboard will one day reach the same level of maturity. Whether it uses the approach currently proposed by Apple, or as-yet-unseen new technology, all three problems can be solved.

When that happens, Steve's arguments will apply equally to the Mac. When used in clamshell form, the keyboard will present the most appropriate layout for the task at hand. When we just want one large screen — whether for watching a film or drawing with an Apple Pencil — we simply unfold it and gain twice the screen area.

So I fully accept that the first-generation product may have been put on hold for now, but that absolutely does not mean it has been cancelled. This is a technology whose time will come.

Those are my thoughts — what are yours? Please share them in the comments.
